top_choice_rationale: P003 credits the demand-estimation core of structural IO (Berry 1994; Berry, Levinsohn and Pakes 1995) to Pakes, Berry and Levinsohn. The method made it possible to estimate substitution patterns, markups and welfare from market data with endogenous prices and heterogeneous consumers. After about thirty years of extension and criticism it is routine in merger review, antitrust, trade, health and environmental economics, so the record is mature. The three-person credit matches the originating papers, and a citation limited to demand estimation avoids an arbitrary cut. The main weaknesses are that it is chiefly methodological and that results depend on functional-form and instrument assumptions. I rank P001 (Kiyotaki and Moore) second because its two-person attribution is cleaner and it has nearly three decades of influence. I find the distinction from the 2022 bank-run prize credible. Its weaknesses are indirect empirical validation and the exclusion of Gertler and Gilchrist. P002 (Autor, Dorn and Hanson, trade-shock evidence) is credibly identified and well attributed, but it is about a decade younger and its shift-share inference and magnitudes are still debated. I rank no award last because at least three shortlisted parts meet the standard of a prize-worthy, attributable achievement. Support counts played no role in the ranking.
recusal_note: No profile-based tie to Pakes, Berry, Levinsohn, Kiyotaki, Moore, Autor, Dorn or Hanson is apparent. My field (industrial organization and trade) is close to P003, which may bias my weighting. I co-authored with chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen (IJIO 2026); neither is a candidate, though Hassler supports P001. My spouse's public political role is noted as a public fact only, with no apparent bearing on this ballot.
